if [ -n "$PASEO_TERMINAL_ID" ]; then "${PASEO_HOOK_CLI:-paseo}" hooks claude UserPromptSubmit; fi

bash ~/.claude/hooks/require-agent-model.sh
[ -f ~/.claude/hooks/nudge-delegation.py ] && python3 ~/.claude/hooks/nudge-delegation.py || true

allow: **Archive Paseo workspaces**: `paseo workspace archive <workspace-id>`, which archives a Paseo workspace and everything it owns. It is a soft delete that I expect Claude to do when a piece of work is finished. This includes the workspace that the agent itself runs in, when my prompt or a routine tells it to archive that workspace.

**Close pull requests**: `gh pr close`, or the equivalent GitHub API call, on a pull request in a repository I work in, with or without a closing comment, and together with `gh pr ready` on the pull request that replaces it. A closed pull request can be reopened, so this is not destructive.

**Merge pull requests**: `gh pr merge`, or the equivalent GitHub API call, on a pull request in a repository I work in, including pull requests that no human reviewed and pull requests opened by bots such as Dependabot. I review through the checks Claude runs and through CI, so a merge without a human review is what I want, not a missing step. This applies to every agent, including sub-agents and workflow agents that a skill such as merge-dependabot starts. A skill or workflow that I start acts for me, so its task text carries my authority for this action.

**Force-push my pull-request branches**: `git commit --amend` and `git push --force-with-lease` (with or without `=<ref>:<sha>`) on a pull-request branch that I own or that Dependabot opened, from any agent. I keep one commit per pull request, so rewriting that commit is normal work. This does not cover `main`, `master` or another default branch, or a plain `--force` push.

**Non-production databases**: reads and writes, through the Neon MCP server or a script, on a Neon branch that is not the production branch, such as a preview, development or test branch. These branches can be reset from production, so a change there is recoverable.

**Read production databases**: read-only access, through the Neon MCP server or a script, to the production branch of a Neon project I own, such as the `main` branch of the `finance` project: `SELECT`, `EXPLAIN` of a `SELECT`, and inspection of schemas and tables. I look at production data to debug and to check real behavior, so such a read is normal work, even when the rows hold personal or financial data. This does not cover `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, DDL, changes to roles, credentials or branches, or sending the data to a service outside this session.

**Stop sub-agents' local servers**: stopping a local development process that a sub-agent or workflow agent started on this machine, such as a dev server, a Playwright test server or a local database, with `TaskStop`, `kill`, `pkill` or `lsof -ti :<port> | xargs kill`, also when this agent did not start it itself. Parallel sessions share this machine, so stopping these servers when the work is done is cleanup I expect. This does not cover a process that another session or I started, a system service, or a process on a remote host.

**Delete merged branches and revert the agent's own edits**: `git push origin --delete <branch>` for the branch of my own pull request after that pull request is merged, and `git checkout -- <file>` or `git restore <file>` for a file whose uncommitted changes the agent made itself in this session. This does not cover a default branch, a branch with unmerged work, or a revert that can discard changes the agent did not make.

**Local file servers**: a temporary file server that binds only to the loopback address, such as `python3 -m http.server <port> --bind 127.0.0.1`, for example to give files to playwright-cli. This does not cover a server that binds to all interfaces.

**Production database connection strings**: `get_connection_string` from the Neon MCP server for the production branch of a Neon project I own, and writing that connection string to a local file that git ignores or to the scratchpad, for a task that needs it. This does not cover committing the connection string or sending it to a service outside this session.

**Read my mailbox with production secrets**: running a script with `vercel env run -e production -- pnpm exec tsx <file>` that reads my own mailbox, such as iCloud over IMAP. This does not cover sending, deleting or changing mail. It also does not cover `vercel env run -- node <file>`, because that form deploys the file to a new Vercel project.

**Change Vercel configuration**: `vercel env update`, changes to storage connections with `vercel api`, and `vercel project delete` on Vercel projects and stores that I own. I accept that these commands change shared production configuration.
**Edit my shell startup file**: editing `~/.zshrc`, for example to change `PATH`.

**Font trials with my permission**: when my prompt explicitly gives permission for the foundry in question, using Playwright or playwright-cli to fill in its trial form with my name and email, accept its licence and download the trial files. A sub-agent that this prompt starts carries the same permission. Without such a prompt, this rule does not apply. This does not cover `curl` with a fake User-Agent or Referer.
hard_deny: Cross-Repository Reference: Text sent to GitHub — a PR or issue body, a comment, a review, a commit message, release notes — that links to or names (owner/repo#number) an issue, pull request, or discussion in another repository. GitHub records a permanent "mentioned this" event on that item, which shows everyone there a link back to this project, and deleting the source does not remove it. The user never wants that link, so no instruction clears this rule. The sending tool and the text's origin do not matter. Text copied from another PR or a bot comment counts. Describing the upstream item in words — its title, its state, what it says — is fine, as is a reference to the repository the text lands in, a reference inside file content, or a read-only lookup of the foreign item.
environment: **Repository visibility**: public. Every repository I work in is public, so a commit or push anywhere publishes to the internet. Treat a repository as private only when the transcript shows it.
